basics.summary: Git tracks content through three areas (working tree, index and repository), and most everyday surprises come from forgetting which area a command touches, how ignore rules match, or which config level wins.
points: `git add` copies a file's current content into the index; a commit records the index, not your working tree, so edits made after `git add` are not included until you add again.
`git status --short` has two columns: index vs HEAD, then working tree vs index. `AM`, `MM`, `AD` and `R ` each describe a precise state.
`git commit -a` and `git add -u` cover tracked files only; `git add -A` also stages new files and lets status detect renames.
`.gitignore` only affects untracked files. To stop tracking a committed file, run `git rm --cached` and commit, and treat any committed secret as leaked.

Ignore patterns: a leading or middle slash anchors to the `.gitignore`'s directory, a trailing slash matches directories, the last matching line wins, and you can't re-include a file whose parent directory is excluded (use `dir/*` instead).
Config precedence runs system < global < local (< worktree) < `-c` on the command line. `git config --show-origin` and `--show-scope` show where a value comes from.
`.gitattributes` is committed with the project: `text eol=lf`, `binary`, diff and merge drivers, and `export-ignore` apply to everyone, unlike each developer's `core.autocrlf`.
traps: `logs/` followed by `!logs/keep.txt` keeps the file ignored; write `logs/*` then `!logs/keep.txt`.
`git clone --depth 1 ../repo` ignores `--depth` for local paths (use `file://`), and `--depth` implies `--single-branch`.
Git doesn't track empty directories, and it doesn't record renames; rename detection is content-based with a 50% similarity default.
